verdict.tagline: Fast parkour and brutal survival, despite a weak narrative.
for_you_if: you enjoy cooperative open world survival
you like crafting gear and scavenging resources
you want fluid parkour movement mechanics
not_for_you_if: you expect a strong main story
you want the final mission playable in co-op

cohorts.label: 2-20h
cohorts.summary: Players note the predictable plot and forgettable villain in the main story.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the main story features a predictable plot and a clichéd, forgettable villain.

citations.review_text:
Techland nailed the exact formula other survival games miss: making movement itself an absolute blast. Scaling rooftops and vaulting over hordes in the quarantined city of Harran feels fluid, weighty, and endlessly satisfying.

The Good:

Peak Parkour: Getting from point A to point B is never a chore; it’s half the thrill.

Terrifying Nights: By day, you’re a capable scavenger. By night, the Volatiles come out, turning every supply run into pure, heart-pounding panic.

Crunchy Combat: Drop-kicking zombies off roofs and swinging electrified pipes never gets old.

Elite Co-op: Playing the full campaign with friends turns tense escapes into hilarious chaos.

The Bad:

The main story is pretty predictable, with a cliché villain. You're here for the gameplay and atmosphere, not an Oscar-winning script.

Even years later, nothing beats the sheer panic of hearing that night-time chime when you’re miles away from a safe zone. Must-play.

Ten years later and nothing has beaten the first night in Harran. The sun goes down, someone on the radio says "good night, good luck", and suddenly you're running for your life from Volatiles with your heart going crazy. The parkour is amazing once you level up agility, the grappling hook makes you feel like Spider-Man, and the dropkick is the best weapon in the game. Did the whole thing twice in co-op with friends and it's even better that way. The story is pretty cheesy and Rais is a forgettable villain, and the first few hours are slow until Crane stops being so weak. Don't skip The Following, the buggy is a blast.

single_points.text: One reviewer says the pacing is awful with a long jumping tutorial, ill-timed crafting and weapon tutorials, and hours of gameplay before it gets interesting.

citation.review_text:
Pacing of this game is just awful. Two hours of gameplay, and literally nothing is happening.

First a basic tutorial on jumping. It lasts about 20 minutes, which is about 18 minutes longer than it needs to be. Second, a basic tutorial on crafting. Ill-timed, as you have very limited crafting items at this point. Then a tutorial on weapons - again, the timing is awful, because you've got almost nothing in your inventory. Then you parkour around the city, running errands. 

I'm unsure why the reviews are so positive - I'm guessing that if I sink enough time into the game, it gets better? I'm out, though.  There's better gaming experiences to be had - I know, because I've played many games that don't require hours and hours of gameplay before they get interesting.

Legendary weapons are useless they break after one elite fight. Just trash, Its so bad an in depth review is worth little time. Do not wait for sale as $7 does not make it worth it.

cohorts.label: 20-100h
cohorts.summary: Crafting and weapon durability shape the loop, though side objectives and certain enemy behaviors draw complaints.

claims.claim: Side quests and certain mission objectives can feel repetitive or unnecessarily drawn-out.

citations.review_text:
In Dying Light I was most drawn in by the story. From the very beginning you can feel the time pressure and how much is at stake. We are trying to save the city ourselves and the people we meet along the way. It is not just about surviving another night. You start to care about what happens to the characters and whether you can help them.
A big plus is simply getting around Harran. Jumping across rooftops and skillfully avoiding zombies is a lot of fun and during the day you can explore the city more calmly and look for supplies. Everything changes after dark. A simple trip back to a safe zone can turn into a frantic escape and going out at night is genuinely tense. I also like developing skills and upgrading weapons. The character becomes more capable over time but the city can still surprise you.
Not all side quests are equally interesting and some activities can get repetitive. The main story the atmosphere and the gameplay make up for those weaker moments. I recommend Dying Light to anyone who likes zombie games but especially to those who appreciate a strong story and exploration.

Dying Light takes players into the quarantined city of Harran, delivering an intense blend of first-person parkour, brutal melee combat, and survival horror. Stepping into the shoes of undercover agent Kyle Crane, the game immediately hooks you with its sense of verticality and constant danger, offering an engaging and adrenaline-fueled open-world experience.

[h2]Story and Setting[/h2]
Set in a sun-drenched yet devastated Middle Eastern metropolis overrun by a mysterious virus, the narrative centers on Crane’s mission to infiltrate the local survivor factions and retrieve sensitive files. While the main plot relies on familiar zombie-apocalypse tropes, the setting itself feels gritty, lived-in, and rich with environmental storytelling. Side quests add extra color to the world, though some missions can feel unnecessarily drawn-out with repetitive tasks that occasionally stall the momentum.

[h2]Gameplay Mechanics and Combat[/h2]
The standout feature of Dying Light is its fluid parkour system. Scaling buildings, leaping across rooftops, and escaping hordes feels natural and deeply satisfying, especially once you unlock advanced agility skills and the grappling hook. Combat is equally visceral—improvised weapons break down, hits carry real weight, and crafting electrified or flaming modifications keeps encounters fresh and strategic.

[h2]Graphics and Atmosphere[/h2]
Visually, the game holds up remarkably well. The contrast between scavenging through dilapidated slums in broad daylight and fighting to survive pitch-black nights creates an unmatched atmosphere. When the sun goes down, dynamic lighting, eerie audio design, and relentless Volatile hunters transform the game into a genuinely terrifying survival experience.

[h2]Pacing and Travel Limitations[/h2]

citations.review_text:
pros: nice story, good voice acting, amazing parkour (satisfying asf and the best i've ever played in a videogame), the night is insane and cool (scares the shit out of me every time) and the sound design is cool too

cons: the combat system is absolutely trash, one of the worst i've ever seen in a game; the enemies are tanky as shit, most of the fights with the zombies are boring as hell, unless you are against human enemies, which is less bad but somehow they have infinite throwable items that just ragebait me

if i based my review on the number of pros which is much bigger than the cons, i'd absolutely recommend it. but unfortunately the only downside (the combat) really overshadows all the good stuff in the game and significantly spoils the fun

[b]Dying Light[/b] is a game I've tried to get into several times, originally after receiving recommendations from friends. Having played Dead Island before it, I was already familiar with the general formula. Both games share similar gameplay foundations, as Dying Light was developed by the core team behind the original Dead Island. However, they are separate intellectual properties with no shared narrative universe. Dying Light attempts to establish its own identity through parkour and a stronger focus on survival.

The parkour system is easily the game's strongest feature. Moving across rooftops, jumping between buildings and navigating the city is genuinely enjoyable. However, I find it rather ironic that I have more fun moving around the map than actually fighting zombies. The parkour is a great addition, but it doesn't compensate for the weaknesses of the combat system.

My biggest problem is the lack of satisfying physical interactions with enemies. In a zombie game, I expect attacks to have visible impact, with blood, gore, dismemberment and convincing reactions to different weapons. Dead Island 2 is a much better example of what I expect from this type of combat. In Dying Light, regular zombies often feel too static, with limited reactions to attacks. Human enemies are even worse: you can hit them in the head with a heavy weapon and they barely react, while they can dodge attacks and perform elaborate movements that the player cannot. It is frustrating when enemies seem to have more convincing combat mechanics than the character you're controlling.

The encounter design also becomes repetitive. Most regular zombies aren't particularly threatening, with the more dangerous infected appearing primarily at night. Missions are scattered across large areas, requiring constant travelling and backtracking. Even clearing an area of zombies feels pointless when they eventually respawn. I would have preferred a system where our actions had some lasting impact on the w…

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the final mission of the main story cannot be played in co-op mode.

citations.review_text:
A legendary experience that was even better with a friend.

I finally got around to playing Dying Light in 2026, thanks to a friend who introduced me to the game. Funny enough, we originally planned to play it together four years ago, and I honestly wish we had done it back then. Better late than never!

Dying Light is an incredible experience. There is something special about the way this game combines parkour, survival, exploration and combat. Moving across rooftops, escaping infected, exploring Harran and constantly looking for ways to survive never really gets boring. The atmosphere is fantastic, especially when night falls and everything suddenly becomes much more dangerous. The game does a great job of making you feel like you are never completely safe.

I particularly enjoyed the freedom the game gives you. Whether you are exploring, completing side quests, upgrading your equipment or simply running around the city, there is always something to do. The combat is satisfying, the progression feels rewarding, and the overall gameplay loop kept me interested from beginning to end.

[spoiler]Playing it with a friend made the experience even more memorable. We managed to enjoy the game together, although unfortunately, we couldn't complete the final mission of the main story or the final mission of the DLC in co-op. We even tried using mods to make it possible, but had no luck.[/spoiler] His PC is also a little older, so we had to work around a few limitations. Nevertheless, I'm grateful we finally got to experience this game together.

I also want to give credit to Techland for creating something that still feels so enjoyable years after its release. Dying Light has a special charm that makes you want to keep coming back for more.

Overall, I loved practically every moment of this journey. I'm genuinely glad my friend introduced me to this masterpiece, and I only wish we had played it four years earlier.

If you enjoy open-world zombie games with satisfying parkou…

Despite its (imo) lackluster story and characters, Dying Light is one of my favorite games for its incredible gameplay and survival mechanics. It's tied with Project Zomboid for the best zombie survival game out there, but I wouldn't compare the two because they're so different. Most of my playtime is from the online PvP mode which kept me up all night back when I played it. Even if you dislike the PvP mode, the singleplayer campaign (which supports co-op!!!) is an amazing experience. My only issue besides the story is that the final mission can NOT be played in co-op for SOME reason and it's honestly such a shame.

single_points.text: One reviewer says that weapon durability gets annoying.

citation.review_text:
Dying Light taught me that cardio is important, rooftops are essential, and going outside after sunset is a decision best left to people with a death wish.

Welcome to Harran, where the zombies are dangerous, but your own confidence is usually what gets you killed.

The parkour is fantastic, melee combat feels brutal and satisfying, and the day-night cycle remains one of the best mechanics in survival horror. Few games can turn a casual supply run into a full-blown panic attack quite like this one.

The story is decent rather than exceptional, weapon durability gets annoying, and some missions become repetitive. But the atmosphere, exploration, and co-op chaos more than make up for it.

Has it aged well? Exceptionally. The visuals still hold up, movement remains excellent, and nighttime is genuinely terrifying. Many newer zombie games still struggle to recreate that feeling.

Ratings:

Gameplay: 9.5/10

Story: 7/10

Graphics: 8.5/10

Atmosphere: 10/10

Enjoyment: 9.5/10

Dying Light didn't need the biggest map or the most complicated RPG systems. It understood something much simpler: zombies should be terrifying, movement should be fun, and surviving the night should feel like an achievement.

Overall: 9/10 | Highly Recommended
